summary: Permitted to speak before Agrippa, Paul stretches out his hand and expresses gratitude for a judge familiar with Jewish customs and disputes. He roots his case in Pharisaic life and the hope of God's promise to the twelve tribes, asking why resurrection should be judged incredible. He confesses persecuting Jesus-followers and retells the heavenly encounter as a prophetic commission: Jesus appoints him servant and witness and sends him to open eyes, turn people from darkness, and bring Gentiles into sanctified inheritance. Paul says he obeyed by preaching repentance expressed in deeds. Festus calls him mad; Paul answers soberly and appeals to Agrippa's knowledge of the prophets. The rulers agree he has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment and could have been released if he had not appealed.
whyItMatters: Paul's most polished defense turns trial into testimony without evading his violent past. Resurrection is framed as Israel's promised hope, Gentile mission as a prophetic call, and repentance as a life that produces fitting deeds. The hearing exposes a final legal irony: every elite listener can recognize innocence, but the machinery of appeal and political custody continues toward Rome.

context.author: The Luke–Acts narrator presenting Paul's climactic defense before Judean and Roman elites
context.audience: Readers comparing the third call account and seeing Israel's hope carried toward imperial witness
context.date: Near the end of Paul's Caesarean imprisonment
context.setting: Festus's Caesarean audience hall before Agrippa II, Bernice, officers, and civic leaders
context.literaryForm: Forensic-apologetic speech, call narrative, prophetic commission, interruption, and elite verdict

outline.heading: Paul locates his trial within Pharisaic resurrection hope
Paul confesses persecution and recounts Jesus's commission
Paul describes obedient repentance preaching and scriptural witness
Festus interrupts, Paul appeals to Agrippa, and the rulers affirm innocence

keyVerses.text: But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen and of the things which I will reveal to you;
keyVerses.why: The encounter appoints Paul to continuing service and testimony, not private spiritual prestige.

keyVerses.text: but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
keyVerses.why: Paul summarizes mission as ordered witness and repentance made visible in deeds.

keyVerses.text: Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.”
keyVerses.why: Paul's aim is the hearers' freedom in faith, not replication of his imprisonment.

questions.question: Why is Paul glad to speak before Agrippa?
questions.answer: Agrippa knows Jewish customs and disputed questions, unlike Festus, who admits confusion. Paul's courteous exordium seeks an informed hearing without Tertullus's extravagant flattery. His extended hand follows conventional oratorical posture, showing that Spirit-led witness can use learned public rhetoric.

questions.question: What is ‘the hope of the promise’ to the twelve tribes?
questions.answer: Paul identifies resurrection with the fulfillment Israel's twelve-tribe people hope to attain through earnest worship. The phrase treats dispersed Israel as a continuing whole and Paul as accused for a Jewish hope, not as founder of a foreign anti-Jewish religion. His question makes divine resurrection the plausible extension of belief in Israel's God.

questions.question: Why does Paul describe his former zeal so severely?
questions.answer: He says he imprisoned saints, cast a vote or gave approval when they were killed, punished them through synagogues, tried to force blasphemy, and pursued them abroad in furious rage. The confession makes grace costly and public; Paul does not excuse violence as sincere zeal. His authority as witness includes truthful acknowledgment of harm.

questions.question: Why does this call account differ from Acts 9 and 22?
questions.answer: This version places all companions falling, gives the voice a Hebrew/Aramaic setting, includes ‘kick against the goads,’ and puts the full Gentile commission directly in Jesus's speech rather than through Ananias and a later temple vision. Ancient speakers reshape true stories for audience and purpose. The common core remains, while differences show Luke has composed three rhetorical retellings, not copied a fixed transcript.

questions.question: What does ‘kick against the goads’ mean?
questions.answer: A kentron is a sharp prod used to drive an animal; kicking it only wounds the resisting animal. The proverb was familiar in Greek literature and here portrays Saul's persecution as futile resistance to divine direction. Its use in the Semitic-language heavenly speech is a literary way of making the point to Agrippa's Hellenistic court.

questions.question: Does ‘open their eyes’ make Paul the one who saves people?
questions.answer: The commission uses prophetic servant language: Paul is sent so hearers turn from darkness and Satan's authority to God, receive forgiveness, and share an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Jesus. The messenger opens eyes through testimony, but the gift, transfer, forgiveness, and inheritance belong to divine action.

questions.question: What are ‘works worthy of repentance’?
questions.answer: Axios means fitting or corresponding. Deeds do not purchase repentance; they embody the changed direction Paul proclaims. His mission summary joins metanoein, turning to God, and practice, blocking both empty verbal profession and moral achievement detached from grace.

questions.question: Why does Festus call Paul mad?
questions.answer: Paul's resurrection claim, scriptural synthesis, and intense learning sound like mania to the Roman governor. Paul answers that he speaks words of truth and sōphrosynē—sound-mindedness or sobriety—and notes that the public events were not done in a corner. Festus's interruption dramatizes the cultural translation gap.

questions.question: Did Agrippa say ‘almost you persuade me to be a Christian’?
questions.answer: The Greek en oligō is ambiguous: ‘in a short time,’ ‘with little effort,’ or possibly an ironic ‘you think you can quickly make me a Christian.’ Paul's response deliberately takes both ‘little and much’ and turns the exchange into prayer for every hearer. The verse should not be built on one sentimental English rendering alone.

questions.question: Could Paul really have been freed after appealing?
questions.answer: Agrippa says he could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. Whether Festus legally could cancel an accepted appeal is uncertain, and political opposition remained. Narratively the verdict again establishes innocence while the appeal supplies the route promised to Rome; legal irony, not proven strategic error, closes the scene.

glossary.def: Sharp prod used to drive an animal; resisting it becomes an image of self-defeating opposition.
Sound-mindedness, sobriety, or self-control; Paul's answer to Festus's charge of madness.
Ambiguous phrase meaning in a short time, with little, or almost; central to Agrippa's reply.
